name: Harsiddhi Mata Temple, Ujjain
deity: Goddess Harsiddhi, worshipped as Mahakali and Mangalachandika, the Shakti of Ujjain
period: Ancient Shakti Peetha of Avanti, one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas, linked by tradition to King Vikramaditya; the present temple is a Maratha-era reconstruction
dynasty: Maratha-era reconstruction; tradition credits the legendary Vikramaditya
style: Maratha-influenced temple architecture of the Malwa region
summary: Harsiddhi Mata is the guardian goddess of Ujjain, sung as Mahakali among the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas and remembered as the family deity of King Vikramaditya, her twin lamp pillars glowing each evening a short walk from the Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga.

sections.history: Ujjain, the ancient Avanti on the banks of the Shipra, has been a great city of pilgrimage for well over two thousand years, and within it the shrine of Harsiddhi is counted among the most revered seats of the Mother. In the stotram attributed to Adi Shankara, which names the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas, Ujjain's verse begins with the invocation of Mahakali. Local tradition holds that the goddess here is Harsiddhi, also called Mangalachandika, and that she was the family deity of the legendary king Vikramaditya, who is said to have brought her worship to his capital. The temple seen today was reconstructed in the Maratha period, but the sanctity of the place is far older, and the shrine has remained in unbroken worship beside the Rudra Sagar tank.
sections.architecture: The temple is built in the Maratha manner, with four entrances facing the four directions and the principal gateway to the east. Its most memorable feature stands just outside the sanctum: two tall lamp pillars, the deep-stambhs, their stone shafts studded with rows of small recesses for oil lamps, which are regarded as fine examples of Maratha craftsmanship and are traditionally credited to Vikramaditya. In the sanctum the goddess is worshipped together with the forms of Annapurna, Mahalakshmi and Mahasaraswati, and a Sri Yantra shrine is honoured within the complex. The carved pillars of the assembly hall are said to preserve older work, lending the compact precinct a quiet depth.
sections.legends: According to the old tale told in the Puranas, Sati gave up her life at her father Daksha's sacrifice, and a grief-stricken Shiva wandered the earth carrying her body. To end his sorrow, Vishnu scattered her form across the land, and wherever a part fell, a Shakti Peetha was born. At Ujjain, local tradition says her elbow fell, though some lists of the peethas name another limb for this city. A second great story belongs to Vikramaditya, who is remembered as the most devoted of the goddess's worshippers. In the tradition he offered his own head to Harsiddhi, and she restored it each time, until the final offering, which she did not return, marking the end of his rule. The lamp pillars are held to be his gift to the Mother.
sections.festivals: Navratri is the heart of the temple's year, kept in both Chaitra in March or April and Ashwin in September or October. During these nine nights the two lamp pillars are lit from base to crown, and the whole precinct glows with a golden light that draws pilgrims from across Madhya Pradesh. Even on ordinary days the evening aarti is accompanied by the lighting of the lamps, and the morning aarti opens the day with devotion. Confirm dates and aarti times locally, as they follow the Hindu calendar and change during festivals.
sections.experience: Harsiddhi is most rewarding in the early evening. Walk the short lane from the Mahakaleshwar temple, pass beneath the gateway, and stand before the two great lamp pillars as the first flames are lit and climb upward in the dusk. Then enter for darshan of the goddess, whom devotees approach for protection, strength and the fulfilment of vows. The precinct is small and often crowded, especially in Navratri, but the glow of the lamps and the sound of the aarti bring a feeling of warm and living devotion that visitors carry away long after.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to evening, with morning aarti around 7 to 8 AM and evening aarti with the lighting of the lamp pillars around 6 to 7 PM; hours are longer during Navratri. Confirm timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis, kurta-pyjamas or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the courtyard and around the lamp pillars but not inside the sanctum. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands beside the Rudra Sagar tank in the old city of Ujjain, a short walk from the Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga. Ujjain Junction is the nearest railway station, and the city is linked by road with Indore, whose airport is around 55 km away. Auto-rickshaws and e-rickshaws run from the station and bus stand to the temple lanes.
